In this stylized market no promotion pays: profit falls with depth under both policies and under every model, because a discount gives away more margin than it wins in conversions. Our toy does not reproduce a profitable gap, and we did not tune it until it did. Second, at every depth the gap beats the uniform discount, under all three models. The obvious explanation is the reference price: see the full price in one channel, and the discount in the other looks like a gain. The last two columns test that explanation by switching the reference effect off in the *true* model. The gap's advantage roughly *doubles* (0.046 instead of 0.024 at 30%). In this market, then, the gap wins on margin, because fewer sales carry the discount, and the reference effect works against it. With losses weighted twice as heavily as gains, a consumer who has just seen the mini-program's discount registers the app's full price as a loss. A gap creates losses as well as gains. Whether a channel gap gains from the reference effect therefore depends on the gain–loss asymmetry, on how the reference is formed, and on which channel consumers see first. A reader of @zhang2026footprints should look for exactly those estimates behind the 32% gap. Third, the models' errors are not neutral across policies. The MSS estimates overstate profit at every policy (0.219 against 0.164 with no promotion), which is the parameter bias of @tbl-click-search-estimates showing up as money. The reference-free model errs most at deep gaps: it predicts that a 40% gap leaves 0.108 of profit per session when the truth is 0.063, an overstatement of about 70%, against about 25% for the MSS model (0.079). The *drop* from no promotion to a 40% gap tells a different story: the reference-free model gets it almost exactly (0.099 against a true 0.101), while the MSS model overstates it (0.140). Neither model is uniformly better. Which one errs less depends on whether the decision turns on profit levels or on profit differences between policies. A counterfactual is only as good as the parameters that drive the policy being evaluated, which is why papers in this genre report recommendations from the incumbent model alongside their own. Two lessons from building the estimator are worth more than the estimates. First, check the likelihood against the simulator before estimating anything. If the simulator's own taste draws are fed back as a single "draw", every rule must hold, and the negative log-likelihood must fall toward zero as $\rho$ grows. In a pilot run it did. That check verifies the inequalities but not the averaging across draws. A bug in the averaging, where R's `ifelse()` silently collapsed a consumer-by-draw matrix to its first column, left the profile likelihood minimized far from the true intercept and price coefficient. Only profiling each parameter around its true value exposed it. Second, the smoothing scale is a tuning parameter. In the pilot, once the bug was fixed, $\rho = 10$ put the profile minima at or next to the true values, and $\rho = 25$ did worse. This is why the literature picks $\rho$ by Monte Carlo [@ursu2025sequential]. The full script simulates the footprints, estimates both models, and runs the counterfactual. It is shipped with the book as `replication/multichannel-search/mss_simulate_estimate.R` and is not run at render time. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Not run at render time: see replication/multichannel-search/mss_simulate_estimate.R source("replication/multichannel-search/mss_simulate_estimate.R") ``` ::: ## Deep Sequence Models {#sec-click-deep} The classical methods above impose structure: a Markov chain assumes limited memory, and sequence analysis fixes a dissimilarity metric in advance. *Deep sequence models* invert this, learning a representation of behavior directly from raw event streams with minimal hand-specified structure. This section is conceptual; the models below are described rather than fit, because training them at scale is beyond a runnable book example, but the architectures are the production workhorses of large digital platforms and deserve to be named precisely. *Recurrent neural networks* (RNNs), and their gated variants the LSTM and GRU, process a sequence one event at a time while maintaining a hidden state that summarizes the history seen so far. Unlike a fixed-order Markov chain, an RNN can in principle carry information across arbitrarily long gaps, learning, for example, that a search early in a session conditions the value of a much later product view. RNNs were the first deep architecture to deliver strong session-based recommendation, and sequential recommendation remains a leading application of behavioral sequence modeling [@zheng2023recommending]. *Transformers* replace recurrence with *self-attention*, letting every event attend directly to every other event in the sequence. Self-attention removes the sequential bottleneck of RNNs, parallelizes training, and captures long-range dependencies more effectively, which is why transformer architectures now dominate sequential recommendation and behavioral modeling. The canonical architecture, Vaswani et al., "Attention Is All You Need" (NeurIPS 2017), has no canonical Crossref DOI and is cited by name; its adaptation to user-behavior sequences underlies modern next-item prediction. *Survival and hazard models* address a different target: not the next event but the *timing* of an event, paradigmatically churn. A survival model treats the time until lapse as the object of inference and models the *hazard*, the instantaneous risk of lapsing at time $t$ given survival so far, as a function of behavioral covariates. This is the natural frame for churn and retention precisely because lapse is censored: most customers have not yet churned at the time of analysis, and a survival model uses that censored information correctly where a binary classifier discards it. Behavioral covariates, declining session frequency, shortening visits, shifting activity mix, enter the hazard and yield a continuously updated risk score. The deep-learning extension replaces the linear hazard with a neural network over the event sequence, fusing the representational power of the architectures above with the censoring-aware machinery of survival analysis. A recurring caution governs all of these models, and it is the same caution that governs text and image features elsewhere in this part: a learned representation of behavior is a *generated regressor*. When the output of a sequence model (a churn score, a propensity, an engagement embedding) is fed into a downstream regression or decision, its estimation error can correlate with the outcome, and the standard errors of the downstream model will understate uncertainty unless the generation step is accounted for. Behavioral embeddings are powerful inputs, but they are model outputs first. ## Forecasting Sales from the Clickstream Graph {#sec-click-forecast} Everything so far treats the clickstream as a record of *individual* journeys. A retailer's operations team asks a different question: how many units of each SKU will sell over the next three days? That is an *aggregate* quantity, and the click log bears on it in two ways. First, views and carts precede purchases, so today's browsing is advance demand information about tomorrow's sales. @huang2014clickstream showed that adding clickstream signals to a demand model improves forecasts and lowers inventory cost, and @martinezdealbeniz2020flash used a hierarchical model of sequential shopping decisions to forecast volatile flash-sale demand. Second, shoppers compare. Someone who views four phones and buys one has told the platform that those four are substitutes, and the three that were not bought still carry information about the one that was. Models that forecast each SKU from its own history discard that cross-product signal. @liu2026clickstream turn it into a forecasting architecture, ForecastClickGraph, and the paper is a good specimen of how to put *learned embeddings* to work on a marketing log. Three embeddings are learned in sequence. I walk through them, rebuild the part of the machinery that can be rebuilt without the authors' data, and then read the evidence the way a referee would. ### The Product-Stage Graph {#sec-click-forecast-graph} The unit of the graph is a *product-stage*: "SKU A viewed", "SKU A added to cart" and "SKU A purchased" are three different nodes. A directed edge from node $j$ to node $i$ carries the number of times that day's sessions moved from $j$ to $i$. A view of A followed by a cart-add of A is an *intra-product* edge; a view of A followed by a view of B is an *inter-product* edge. Each day gets its own graph, and each node carries a time series of its daily event counts. The target is the purchase node's series over the next $H$ days, forecast at several quantiles rather than as a single number. On the public data the authors use, the graphs are large and mostly cross-product. The data are a Kaggle log of 285 million events from a Middle Eastern e-commerce platform, October 2019 to April 2020 [@kechinov2020ecommerce]. The holiday subset the paper models holds 38 million sessions over 239,718 SKUs. The average daily graph has about 87,490 nodes and 917,220 edges, and roughly 95% of the edges join *different* SKUs. The transition table is informative on its own. After viewing a SKU, a shopper views another SKU about 50% of the time and carts or buys the same one only 3.58% of the time. After carting, the shopper sticks with it: fewer than 3% move to another SKU. After a purchase, 6.6% go on to view a different product. The funnel is leaky at the top and sticky at the bottom, which is why cross-product edges matter early in the journey and intra-product edges matter late. ### Three Embeddings {#sec-click-forecast-embeddings} **An embedding of each node's history.** An LSTM reads a node's last $T = 7$ daily counts, after each series is rescaled by its median and mean absolute deviation, and its final hidden state is the node's *time-series embedding*. A small MLP maps that embedding to the base forecast: $H$ steps by the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles, produced directly rather than recursively, so errors do not compound across the horizon. All SKUs share one set of weights (*cross-learning*), which is what lets the model forecast SKUs with short histories [@salinas2020deepar]. **An embedding of the neighborhood.** A Graph Transformer layer [@shi2021masked] lets a purchase node attend over its *upstream* neighbors, the view and cart nodes that feed it, including those of other products. Query, key and value vectors are linear maps of the neighbors' time-series embeddings, the edge weight enters the key, and the attention-weighted sum of the values is the *neighbor embedding*. A second MLP turns it into a second set of quantile forecasts. The authors read the attention weight as a proxy for the conversion rate from the upstream node to the purchase node. Because neighbors' views and carts are already partly reflected in the node's own history, adding the neighbor forecast naively would double count, so a sigmoid *gate* computed from all three embeddings shrinks it before it is added. **An embedding of burstiness.** The third piece borrows the burstiness score of @lappas2009burstiness. For a series $y_1,\dots,y_T$, the score at time $t$ is the observed share of the window's total, $y_t / \sum_s y_s$, minus the share expected if the activity were spread evenly, $1/T$. A day with a large positive score is a spike relative to the window. Each node's burstiness series is averaged over its upstream neighbors to form a *neighbor burstiness* series, which a dense layer embeds. A tanh output in $[-1, 1]$ is then multiplied by an exponential moving average of the node's own sales (smoothing factor 0.7) to give a proportional correction to the trend. The logic is that a burst in views and carts across *many* related products is more likely a platform-wide promotion than noise in one series, and it shows up in the neighbors before it reaches purchases. The final forecast is the sum of the base, burst and gated neighbor forecasts, trained on the quantile (pinball) loss of @koenker1978regression summed over quantiles, horizon steps and SKUs. The same architecture accepts a fourth embedding, the one most marketing papers would start with. The authors' appendix adds learned embeddings of brand (5,384 values) and category (142 values), each of dimension 8, with a default vector for the 38% to 41% of products missing the field. It lowers MSE by 2.5% and *raises* SMAPE by 2.7%, which the authors read as noise from the missing metadata. Metadata embeddings are not free when a large share of the metadata is missing. ### Rebuilding the Mechanism {#sec-click-forecast-replicate} The authors' trained model is not available, only the manuscript, and the 285-million-row log is too large for a book that renders offline. What *can* be rebuilt exactly is the arithmetic the paper walks through in its Figure 3, and the logic of the burst correction can be checked on a simulation built to contain it. The first lines of the chunk below reproduce the paper's worked example: for a SKU-A purchase series of $(9, 14, 17)$ the scaled series is $(-1.875, 0, 1.125)$, the burstiness scores are $(-0.108, 0.017, 0.092)$, and a forecast of 8 against an outcome of 10 costs 1.5 on the pinball loss at $q = 0.75$. The rest simulates 300 SKUs over 70 days in which a latent demand lift shows up in views and carts the same day and reaches purchases a day later, then compares a trend-only forecast with one corrected by neighbor burstiness (@tbl-click-forecast-sim). ::: {#tbl-click-forecast-sim .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Simulated one-day-ahead purchase forecasts with and without the neighbor-burstiness correction. MSE on held-out days.'} ```{.r .cell-code} robust_scale <- function(y) { m <- median(y); (y - m) / mean(abs(y - m)) } burstiness <- function(y) { if (sum(y) == 0) rep(0, length(y)) else y / sum(y) - 1 / length(y) } pinball <- function(f, y, q) q * pmax(y - f, 0) + (1 - q) * pmax(f - y, 0) # The worked example from the paper's Figure 3 yA <- c(9, 14, 17) round(robust_scale(yA), 3) #> [1] -1.875 0.000 1.125 round(burstiness(yA), 3) #> [1] -0.108 0.017 0.092 pinball(8, 10, 0.75) #> [1] 1.5 # --- A product-stage simulation: 300 SKUs, 70 days --------------------------- set.seed(2026) P <- 300; D <- 70; T0 <- 7 promo_platform <- c(30:32, 55:57) # platform-wide grand promotions base <- exp(rnorm(P, 2.2, 0.8)) # SKU popularity shock <- matrix(rbinom(P * D, 1, 0.01), P, D) # idiosyncratic SKU promotions shock[, promo_platform] <- 1 lift <- matrix(0, P, D) for (t in 1:D) { lift[, t] <- 1 + 2.5 * shock[, t] + if (t > 1) 0.8 * shock[, t - 1] else 0 } view <- matrix(rpois(P * D, 6 * base * lift), P, D) cart <- matrix(rpois(P * D, 0.4 * base * lift), P, D) purch <- matrix(rpois(P * D, base * cbind(1, lift[, -D])), P, D) # one-day lag burst_ts <- function(y) { # window-T0 burstiness, one score per day out <- rep(NA_real_, length(y)) for (t in T0:length(y)) out[t] <- burstiness(y[(t - T0 + 1):t])[T0] out } # NeighBurst: mean burstiness of the upstream nodes (view and cart) neigh <- (t(apply(view, 1, burst_ts)) + t(apply(cart, 1, burst_ts))) / 2 ema <- function(y, lam = 0.7) { e <- y[1]; for (v in y[-1]) e <- lam * e + (1 - lam) * v; e } days <- T0:(D - 1) Em <- t(sapply(1:P, function(i) sapply(days, function(t) ema(purch[i, (t - T0 + 1):t])))) target <- purch[, days + 1] Nb <- neigh[, days] ratio <- pmax(pmin(target / pmax(Em, 1) - 1, 1), -1) train <- days <= 45 # Burst correction: regress next-day deviation from trend on neighbor burstiness correct <- function(Nb) { fit <- lm(c(ratio[, train]) ~ c(Nb[, train])) pmax(Em * (1 + pmax(pmin(coef(fit)[1] + coef(fit)[2] * Nb, 1), -1)), 0) } adj <- correct(Nb) adj_pl <- correct(apply(Nb, 2, sample)) # placebo: shuffle across SKUs within day is_burst <- matrix(rep((days + 1) %in% c(promo_platform, promo_platform + 1), each = P), P) test <- matrix(rep(!train, each = P), P) mse <- function(f, m) mean((f[test & m] - target[test & m])^2) res <- rbind( "Trend only (EMA of own sales)" = c(mse(Em, is_burst | !is_burst), mse(Em, is_burst), mse(Em, !is_burst)), "Trend + neighbor burstiness" = c(mse(adj, is_burst | !is_burst), mse(adj, is_burst), mse(adj, !is_burst)), "Placebo: neighbor signal shuffled across SKUs" = c(mse(adj_pl, is_burst | !is_burst), mse(adj_pl, is_burst), mse(adj_pl, !is_burst)) ) colnames(res) <- c("All test days", "Promotion days", "Other days") knitr::kable(round(res, 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | | All test days| Promotion days| Other days| |:---------------------------------------------|-------------:|--------------:|----------:| |Trend only (EMA of own sales) | 300.2| 1084.9| 143.3| |Trend + neighbor burstiness | 110.7| 389.5| 55.0| |Placebo: neighbor signal shuffled across SKUs | 151.8| 483.9| 85.4| ::: ::: On the simulated promotion days the corrected forecast cuts MSE from about 1,085 to 390, and the gain is not confined to promotions. Part of that is the design: the burst signal here is a clean upstream measure of a latent lift, which real clickstreams only approximate, so the magnitude says nothing about the paper's data. The placebo row is the more useful one. Shuffling the neighbor signal across SKUs *within each day* removes the SKU-specific information but keeps the day's platform-wide level, and it still recovers a large part of the gain (promotion-day MSE of 484). In this world, most of what the burst module buys is the platform-wide promotion signal, and only the remainder is SKU-specific. That is the intuition the authors give for averaging burstiness over many neighbors, and it suggests a test they could add on the real data: shuffle within day and see how much of the paper's 7.8% burst-period ablation effect survives. ### What the Evidence Shows {#sec-click-forecast-evidence} All figures here come from the author-accepted manuscript; the published version may differ in detail. The comparison is organized as a ladder of *information sets*, which is the best design choice in the paper. Rung one forecasts a SKU from its own sales (Prophet [@taylor2018forecasting], DeepAR, NHITS [@challu2023nhits], Transformer and Informer variants, LSTM). Rung two adds the SKU's own view and cart counts as covariates. Rung three adds neighbors through a graph layer (GAT, GraphSAGE, Graph Transformer). Rung four interleaves graph convolution with recurrence (T-GCN, GConvGRU, GConvLSTM, GC-LSTM). Each rung isolates what an extra layer of the data contributes, so the reader can see which source of information the gain comes from. On the October-to-November test, the proposed model's MSE is 428.1, against 505.9 for the best univariate model (an LSTM), 487.2 for the best covariate model (NHITS), 480.6 for the best static graph model (GAT) and 473.8 for the best dynamic one (T-GCN). The "10% to 28%" in the abstract spans the gap to T-GCN (about 10%) and the gap to Prophet (28%), so the honest summary against a strong deep baseline is a reduction in MSE of roughly 10%. The SMAPE gaps are smaller: the model is under one SMAPE point ahead of every covariate model and of GC-LSTM, GConvGRU and GConvLSTM, while T-GCN, the best baseline on MSE, is 1.4 points behind it on SMAPE (33.5% against 32.1%). Four further results carry the argument. - **Bursts.** The 21 promotion days account for 52% of holiday-season sales. On those days the four strongest models have MSE above 1,400, against about 60 on normal days. The proposed model's burst-period MSE is 1,466 against 1,673 for GAT. - **Ablation.** Dropping the burst module raises overall MSE by 1.5% and burst-period MSE by 7.8%. Dropping the neighbor embedding raises overall MSE by 6.6%. Dropping both raises it by 18.2% and returns exactly the LSTM's 505.9, as it should, since what remains is the LSTM base. - **A visible mechanism.** The learned weight on the neighbor forecast rises from about 0.1 before the November promotion to about 0.4 during it, and the burst multiplier is positive during promotions and often negative right after, consistent with the stockpiling dip described in the promotion literature. - **Cold start and decision metrics.** On 4,769 products launched in December, forecast *without retraining*, MSE is 5.22 against 6.22 for the LSTM. At the 90th percentile, the quantile that sets safety stock, the model's quantile loss is 13.7% below the LSTM's. Its 75% quantile forecast covers 68.8% of outcomes, short of the nominal 75% but closer than the benchmarks. ### A Referee's Reading {#sec-click-forecast-critique} The paper is strong, and the places a referee would press are specific. *The headline metric is dominated by a handful of SKUs.* MSE rewards getting the popular SKUs right, and on promotion days the squared errors are in the thousands. The sales distribution is heavily skewed: among active SKU-days the 75th percentile of daily purchases is 3 while the maximum is 4,469. A per-SKU-weighted metric, or the gain broken down by volume decile, would show whether the 10% is broad or concentrated. The connectivity split in the paper's boundary conditions points the same way: a 16% gain over the LSTM on high-connectivity SKUs and 2.4% on low. *The evaluated universe is filtered.* Target SKUs are those with sales on at least half the training days (3,445 in October, 3,251 in November) out of 239,718 in the log. The authors say so and put intermittent demand out of scope, which is fair, but it means the results speak to the head of the catalog. *The significance tests vary the seed, not the world.* Each model is trained 30 times and compared with a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test. That tests whether the difference survives *training* noise. It does not say whether the difference would survive a different month, platform or set of promotions, and the test set is one platform and a few months (the second, non-holiday window, January to April 2020, overlaps the onset of COVID-19). Forecasts for different SKUs on the same promotion day are also strongly dependent, so the effective sample is much smaller than the number of SKU-days. *Attention is not the conversion rate.* The authors read attention weights as proxies for stage-to-stage conversion. Their own Table 2 reports the empirical transition probabilities directly, and those are what the edge weights already encode. The post-hoc analysis in their Appendix 8 examines the neighbor weight and the burst multiplier, not the edge-level attention. Treating attention as a managerial measure of which products lead demand (the paper's search-versus-experience discussion) needs that check first. *Prices and promotion depth are excluded by design.* That is the right choice for a marketplace that cannot see sellers' plans, and it is what lets the model run on a public log. It also means the burst module learns promotion *effects*, not promotion *causes*: it can react to a promotion that has started but cannot plan one. The paper's own boundary condition says that on a reseller platform with promotion calendars, a model with those inputs should win (on promotion information in retail forecasting, see @fildes2022retail). ### Using the Template {#sec-click-forecast-template} The paper is also a template for a *method-for-a-new-data-source* paper at a top operations or information-systems journal. The structure transfers to other behavioral logs, and each piece does a job in the argument. 1. **A new representation of an unstructured trace.** The contribution is the product-stage graph, a way of turning a log into a structure a model can use. A novel network layer is secondary, and here an off-the-shelf Graph Transformer does the attending. 2. **A task-specific module tied to a managerial problem.** The burst module answers one operational problem, promotion spikes, and the ablation shows it earns its place. 3. **A benchmark ladder organized by information set**, so that each rung answers "what does this extra data buy?" rather than "does my model beat everyone's?" 4. **A decision metric next to the statistical one.** Quantile loss, calibration and achieved service level connect the forecast to inventory choices. 5. **Boundary conditions as results.** Sparse graphs, stable demand and available prices are named as conditions under which the method should *not* win, and one (connectivity) is tested. 6. **Public data.** The Kaggle log lets a reader rerun the benchmarks, which is much of why a methods paper is believed. The authors' code was not found alongside the manuscript. The same recipe fits a marketing question. A brand's clickstream, review stream or search-query log can be turned into a graph whose nodes are product-stages, queries or creators, with learned embeddings of each node's history and neighborhood (@sec-graph-embeddings). If those embeddings feed a downstream causal regression, the generated-regressor caution of @sec-click-deep applies: a forecasting embedding is a model output, and the estimation error does not disappear in the second stage. For the writing side of the template, see the design-science method-paper structure in @sec-sw-design-science. ## Attribution {#sec-click-attribution} Attribution deserves separate treatment because it is the application where method choice most directly moves money, and where the gap between convenient heuristics and defensible models is widest. The problem is to distribute credit for a conversion across the touchpoints, channels, ad exposures, and site visits that preceded it. The *heuristic* attribution rules require no model and are correspondingly crude. *Last-touch* assigns all credit to the final touchpoint before conversion; *first-touch* assigns it all to the first; *linear* splits credit equally; *time-decay* weights recent touches more. Each encodes an untested assumption about how influence accrues along a path, and last-touch in particular systematically overcredits the bottom-of-funnel channels that users were always going to reach and undercredits the upper-funnel channels that initiated the journey [@montgomery2004modeling]. The *data-driven* alternatives infer credit from the structure of observed paths. The Markov removal-effect model of @sec-click-removal is the leading example: by defining a channel's value as the conversion lost when its paths are diverted, it credits channels by their causal role *within the observed path structure* rather than by their position [@anderl2016mapping]. A complementary tradition builds explicit measurement models of the multichannel journey: @li2014 model a customer's consideration of channels, visits through them over time, and subsequent purchase, and crucially validate the model against a field experiment, and Abhishek, Fader, and Hosanagar ("The Long Road to Online Conversion," SSRN working paper 2012, DOI `10.2139/ssrn.2158421`) model the path from media exposure to conversion with a hidden-Markov structure over latent journey stages. Closely related work disentangles how channels interact along the path: @dehaan2016effectiveness compare the conversion impact of different online ad forms within a multichannel attribution framework, and @kireyev2016display show that display advertising *dynamically* raises later search activity, so crediting search alone double-undercounts display. Individual-level exposure data let @zantedeschi2017 measure multichannel advertising response jointly across mail and email. The same path logic extends to paid search itself, where keyword-level clickstream supports both reduced-form [@ghose2009empirical] and dynamic structural [@yao2011dynamic] models of sponsored-search performance. The broader digital-marketing framework that situates attribution among the firm's measurement problems is reviewed by @kannan2017. Two cautions apply to every attribution model, heuristic or data-driven. First, attribution is *correlational by default*: a model fit to observed paths recovers associations between touchpoints and conversion, not the counterfactual conversion that would have occurred absent a touchpoint, unless the design supports a causal reading. The strongest attribution work therefore pairs the model with experimental variation, as Li and Kannan (2014) do, rather than resting on observational paths alone. Second, attribution is acutely sensitive to *what is logged*. Touchpoints that go unrecorded, view-through impressions, cross-device journeys, offline exposures, are silently assigned zero credit, biasing the attribution toward the well-instrumented channels. The measurement boundary is the attribution boundary. ## Industry and Production Practice {#sec-click-production} The methods above presuppose a clean event log. In practice that log is the *output* of a substantial data-engineering pipeline, and the integrity of every downstream analysis depends on how that pipeline is built. This section sketches the production reality that academic treatments usually omit, because the failure modes it introduces are precisely the ones that invalidate published-looking results. @fig-clk-pipeline maps the pipeline end to end, from instrumentation to the point-in-time features a model consumes. ```{mermaid} %%| label: fig-clk-pipeline %%| fig-cap: "The production event pipeline. Events flow through a collection layer, often a streaming bus, into a *warehouse* or *lakehouse* where they land as an append-only event table. Discipline at this stage, stable event names, versioned schemas, consistent identifiers, is what makes the log analyzable at all; an event whose semantics drift across an app release silently breaks every longitudinal metric defined on it. *Sessionization* (@sec-click-sessionization) is typically materialized in the pipeline rather than recomputed per analysis, so the timeout rule becomes an organizational commitment baked into derived tables. Identity resolution sits alongside it: stitching a user's events across devices and login states determines whether a cross-device journey appears as one user or several, with direct consequences for attribution and CLV. The *warehouse-to-feature pipeline* turns the raw event table into the columns a model consumes. For each user and a chosen *prediction time*, the pipeline aggregates the history into features, counts, recencies, frequencies, sequence summaries, and embeddings, and joins them to a label observed *after* the prediction time. The discipline that governs this step is the avoidance of *look-ahead leakage*: a feature must be computable using only information available at the prediction time, never information from the future relative to it. Leakage is the dominant failure mode of behavioral modeling in practice and is insidious because it inflates offline metrics, a churn model that accidentally includes a post-churn event as a feature will look superb in backtests and fail in production. The structural guard is a *point-in-time correct* feature store that, for any training example, reconstructs feature values as they would have stood at that example's prediction time, and never later. Two further production realities shape the analysis. Bot and non-human traffic, discussed in @sec-click-applications, must be filtered *before* metrics and models are computed, since uncleaned synthetic traffic corrupts transition matrices, funnels, and attribution alike. And privacy and consent regimes increasingly constrain what may be logged and retained at all: cookie deprecation, consent-gated tracking, and on-device measurement shrink the observable event log, which feeds directly back into the measurement-boundary caution of @sec-click-attribution. The clickstream a model sees is not the behavior that occurred; it is the behavior that was instrumented, permitted, and retained. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Replication resources: clickstream analysis The sessionization, transition-matrix estimation, Markov removal-effect attribution, and sequence-clustering demonstrations in this chapter run on open R packages—base R, `data.table`/`dplyr`, the `markovchain`/`ChannelAttribution` family for path attribution, and `TraMineR` for sequence analysis—which constitute a fully reproducible clickstream toolchain. The empirical studies cited here (e.g., @montgomery2004modeling, @li2014, @bronnenberg2016zooming) rest on proprietary firm clickstream that cannot be redistributed, so public replication packages are rare; the methods, not the data, are the transferable artifact, consistent with the unstructured-data program's emphasis on validated, reproducible measurement [@balducci2018unstructured]. ::: ### The offline clickstream {#sec-click-offline} Everything in this chapter assumes the log exists. Physical retail is the large domain where it does not: a store sees transactions, but not the browsing path, dwell, hesitation, and abandonment that make a clickstream informative in the first place. @li2026videoanalytics close that gap directly, building what they call an **offline clickstream** out of in-store security-camera footage. The pipeline is a stack of computer-vision components rather than a single model: person re-identification to hold a shopper's identity across cameras, trajectory reconstruction to recover the path, pose estimation to capture product interaction and body language, and vision-language models to read the scene. The output is the data structure of @sec-click-structure—a time-ordered sequence of events per visit—recovered from pixels instead of from server logs, and it feeds a transformer-based purchase-prediction model of the kind treated in @sec-click-deep. Against demographic and contextual benchmarks, prediction improves by up to 79% on their key metrics, and simulating five real-time targeting policies gives a 13.1% profit lift for a persuadability-based policy over no targeting. Two cautions travel with the result. The first is that a persuadability policy is a causal object being served by a predictive pipeline: targeting the shoppers most movable, rather than those most likely to buy, requires an uplift estimand (@sec-ai-ml), and the gain reported is a simulation under the model rather than a field-measured lift. The second is that the sensing itself is the intervention the shopper did not consent to in the way a website visitor consents to cookies. The authors describe the design as privacy-conscious, and the substantive point for this chapter is that the privacy constraints of @sec-privacy bind on the *collection* step here, not on the modeling step—which is a different regulatory surface from the one online clickstream work has learned to navigate. ## Frontier and Extensions {#sec-click-frontier} Clickstream analysis is consolidating around a few active frontiers. The first is the move from *hand-engineered behavioral features* to *learned behavioral embeddings*: representing each user by a vector that a sequence model has learned from their raw event history, then reusing that vector across churn, recommendation, and lifetime-value tasks. This mirrors the trajectory of text and image data elsewhere in this part, and it inherits the same generated-regressor caution (@sec-click-deep). A second frontier is *causal* clickstream analysis. The observational, self-selected nature of behavioral logs (@sec-click-applications) means that the most consequential questions, does this navigation cause conversion, does this intervention reduce churn, are causal questions that path models answer only under strong assumptions. Integrating behavioral logs with experimental and quasi-experimental designs, so that the rich sequence data supplies covariates and heterogeneity while the design supplies identification, is where attribution and uplift modeling are heading. A third frontier is *multimodal fusion*. The clickstream is one signal among several: a session also generates text (search queries, reviews), images (products viewed), and, increasingly, voice and video interactions. Joint models that fuse the behavioral sequence with these other modalities, the subject of this part as a whole, promise representations of the customer that no single log could yield. The unifying lesson is the one this part returns to throughout: behavioral logs, like text and images, are unstructured traces that become useful only once turned into learned, lossy features, and those features must be defended as generated regressors before any claim is built on them.
